c.text: Chapter 8 – Criticism, Control, and Ongoing
Pastoral Needs
When one good conversation isn’t the answer
The last chapter dealt with a specific problem between you and a reasonable person. Have that conversation properly and most situations resolve.

This chapter is about the ones that don’t – the ongoing patterns. The member who criticises everything you do. The long-standing volunteer who treats one area of the church as personal property. The person in genuine pain who is absorbing every hour you have.

Criticism, controlling behaviour and ongoing distress need different responses. They can also overlap in the same situation. Describe what is happening and what help is needed rather than assigning a fixed label to the person.
Nehemiah, and the four things opponents do
Nehemiah 4 and 6 contain the best case study in Scripture for handling sustained opposition. Nehemiah is rebuilding Jerusalem’s wall, and Sanballat and Tobiah try four separate tactics.
First, mockery.

In 4:1-3 Sanballat is angry and ridicules the Jews in front of his associates, and Tobiah adds that a fox climbing on the wall would break it down. Nehemiah’s response in verse 4 is to pray, and then in verse 6 the wall reaches half its height, because the people had a mind to work.
Second, the endless invitation to meet.

In 6:2 they ask him to come down to a village on the plain of Ono. Nehemiah recognises they intend harm, and sends the reply in verse 3 that I would engrave on many leaders’ desks: he is doing a great work and cannot come down; why should the work stop while he leaves it to come to them? They sent this same request four times, and four times he answered the same way.
Third, the false accusation in writing.

In 6:5-8 an open letter accuses him of planning rebellion and setting himself up as king. Nehemiah’s reply is one sentence: nothing like what you are saying is happening, you are inventing it in your own head. Then he prays for strength and keeps building.
Fourth – and this is the subtlest – a spiritual-sounding trap.

In 6:10-13 a man named Shemaiah, apparently a prophet, urges Nehemiah to hide in the temple because men are coming to kill him. Nehemiah refuses, and then realises Shemaiah had been hired to frighten him into sinning so they could discredit him.

Four tactics: ridicule, distraction, slander, and pressure dressed up as spiritual counsel. If you lead anything for long, you will meet all four. Nehemiah’s pattern is consistent every time – pray, answer briefly, and do not come down off the wall.
Sorting your critics
Not all criticism is opposition.
Before you file someone under “critic,” sort them.

The faithful critic tells you directly, usually privately, and is often right. This person is a gift, even when the delivery stings. Protect them, thank them, and never punish them for honesty – a leader who does that ends up surrounded by people who agree with everything and warn him about nothing.

Repeated criticism can become disruptive, but frequency alone does not tell you whether the concern is valid. Ask for specific examples, check the substance and set reasonable boundaries around how feedback is raised. Avoid assuming you know the person’s motives.

Anonymous or relayed concerns should be assessed on their content, not dismissed because the person has not approached you. Fear or a power imbalance may explain the route. Invite further information through a safe channel, and refer safeguarding allegations appropriately. Do not demand that someone identify themselves publicly before taking a concern seriously.
For all criticism, ask what is accurate and what needs checking. A poorly delivered complaint can still reveal a serious problem. Address the substance before deciding how to respond to the delivery.
The controller

3 John 9-10 is a short and startling passage. John writes that he had written to the church, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not welcome them. John says that if he comes he will call attention to what Diotrephes is doing – gossiping maliciously, refusing to welcome other believers, and putting out of the church those who want to.
One man, controlling access, controlling reputation, and removing people who crossed him. In an apostolic-era church.

You will recognise the modern version. It is usually attached to a specific territory – the kitchen, the sound desk, the flowers, the accounts – and held for many years. The signs: information is not shared, keys are not handed over, new volunteers mysteriously do not last, and any change is met with “we’ve always done it this way” or with a silence that costs you something.
Three principles for handling it.
Do not fight over the territory.

Change the structure. Written procedures, more than one person trained, rotas set by you, and keys held centrally. Most control depends on a single point of dependency, and you dissolve it by removing the dependency rather than by confronting the person.
Be scrupulously clear about authority.
This is where Chapter 3 pays off. If you do not know exactly what is yours to decide, a controller will find that gap and live in it.
Involve the appropriate leader early.

Clarify your authority before changing systems or addressing entrenched behaviour. If the concern involves your pastor, use a suitable independent route. Titus 3:10-11 gives Paul’s instruction to Titus about a person who is divisive: warn them once, then a second time, and after that have nothing to do with them. And in 2 Timothy 4:14-15 Paul names Alexander the metalworker, says he did him great harm, and tells Timothy to be on his guard against him.
Two things follow from this.

There is a limit – you are not required to absorb divisive behaviour indefinitely. And in a church setting, reaching that limit is a decision for the church’s leadership, not for a new ministry leader acting on his own.
People with ongoing pastoral needs
This one is the hardest, because the person is genuinely hurting and your instinct to help is right.

John 5:1-9 describes Jesus meeting a man who had been unable to walk for thirty-eight years and asking whether he wanted to get well. The man explains the obstacles he faces. Jesus heals him. The passage does not justify treating long-term illness or repeated distress as evidence that someone does not want help.

Listen to the obstacles a person describes before suggesting what they should do. Some barriers require practical support, professional care or changes in circumstances that a short pastoral conversation cannot provide.
A helpful question is: “What support would be useful now, and what has made it hard to access?” Ask with curiosity rather than as a test of the person’s willingness to improve.
Both a sudden crisis and long-term distress deserve care.

Neither requires one leader to become the sole source of support. Repeated crises may signal unmet needs, disability, abuse or other circumstances requiring a broader response. Agree what you can offer and help the person connect with appropriate support.

Galatians 6:2 calls believers to carry one another’s burdens; verse 5 also speaks of personal responsibility. Read together, these verses invite mutual help without pretending that one person can live another’s life. They do not give us a simple test for deciding whose pain is legitimate.
Practically:
Set a shape.
“I can meet for an hour on the first Tuesday of the month” is more sustainable, and more genuinely helpful, than being available at all hours until you quietly stop replying.
Do not be their only support.
Make sure a small group, a couple of mature believers, or the pastoral team is involved. Sole dependence on one leader is bad for them and dangerous for you.
Know where your competence ends.

Where there is depression, trauma, addiction, or anything you are not trained for, encourage professional help alongside spiritual support, and involve your pastor. Saying “I’ll keep walking with you, and I also think you should see a doctor about this” is not a failure of faith. It is honest care. Follow your church’s safeguarding arrangements when meeting with children or adults who may be at risk. Explain confidentiality and its limits. Report concerns through the appropriate safeguarding route; if someone is in immediate danger, contact local emergency services. Do not investigate an allegation yourself or alert the person accused without guidance.
Do not come down off the wall
The single sentence to carry out of this chapter is Nehemiah’s in 6:3. I am doing a great work and I cannot come down.

Unresolved conflict and unmet care needs can consume your attention. Set responsible boundaries and arrange the help required, while continuing to attend to the wider team. Nehemiah’s refusal to meet hostile opponents is not permission to ignore complaints or people in distress.
Answer briefly.
Pray honestly. Then get back on the wall.
